answer_text:
Since \(A\) is real symmetric, the spectral theorem gives an orthogonal matrix \(Q\) such that

\[
A = Q \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n) Q^T,
\]

where \(\lambda_i\in \mathbb{R}\). Hence

\[
A^2 = Q \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1^2,\dots,\lambda_n^2) Q^T.
\]

In the eigenbasis of \(A\), the system

\[
\dot{x}=A^2x
\]

decouples into

\[
\dot{y}_i = \lambda_i^2 y_i,
\qquad
y_i(t)=e^{\lambda_i^2 t}y_i(0).
\]

If some \(\lambda_k\neq 0\), then \(\lambda_k^2>0\), and along the corresponding eigendirection,

\[
\|x(t)\|=e^{\lambda_k^2 t}\|x(0)\|
\]

grows without bound. Therefore, for sufficiently small initial data, solutions can leave any prescribed neighborhood of the origin, so the zero solution is not stable.

Thus stability requires

\[
\lambda_i^2=0 \quad \text{for all } i,
\]

so \(\lambda_i=0\) for all \(i\), meaning

\[
A=0.
\]

Conversely, if \(A=0\), then \(\dot{x}=0\), so every solution is constant and the zero solution is stable.

\[
\boxed{A=0_{n\times n}}
\]

27B·v4.method: Spectral theorem on symmetric A shows A² is PSD; Lyapunov stability of ẋ=A²x forces all eigenvalues of A² to be zero, hence A=0.
